China’s Electric Carmakers Are Running Out of Domestic Buyers
 
Plus, Netanyahu faces a high-stakes showdown over whether he will stay in office, and the brutal Harvard class everyone wants to take
 
 
VCG/GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Good morning. China’s electric vehicles are conquering overseas markets, but back home the industry is heading for a wall.

 

Through September, passenger-car sales in China dropped 22%, putting the market on track for its worst performance since 2014. Ordinarily, this would trigger a massive industry shakeout. But local governments that poured billions into EV startups refuse to let failing plants close. To protect jobs, municipal officials keep dozens of zombie brands on life support. 

 

Desperate for customers, Chinese carmakers are piling into overseas markets with hypercompetitive products. Stephen Wilmot and Katrina Northrop detail this political paralysis that is fueling a massive overcapacity crisis.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party moved into the lead position in the country’s election, denying his opponents a victory but still sitting short of a majority that would return his coalition to power.

 

• The U.S. has told several Gulf Arab countries to be prepared for a short, intense military campaign after the U.S. midterm elections, people briefed on the conversations said.

 

• President Trump rallied in support of GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton, and his Democratic opponent James Talarico held an event just 3 miles away. Both were making a final push for support before the midterms.

 

• To gain re-election, Maine Sen. Susan Collins must navigate a polarized electorate, anger over inflation and fallout from the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision overturning Roe vs. Wade.

 

• The law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges is hemorrhaging top lawyers, has no clear succession plan after its incoming chair declined to step into the role, and has engaged a bankruptcy lawyer for advice.

 

• Tal and Oren Alexander, who were once highflying luxury brokers, and their brother Alon were each sentenced to 30 years in prison for sex trafficking.

• Stocks Spencer Jakab is watching: It was Taco Tuesday for Pentair, the S&P 500’s top performing stock. Pentair’s swimming-pool customers are still struggling, but the water technology company’s shares jumped on upbeat guidance for its data-center cooling business. That’s thanks in part to the acquisition of Taco Group Holdings, which closed this month. (Get Spencer’s Markets A.M. newsletter in your inbox.)

 

• With doubts swirling about the sustainability of the AI build out, banks aren’t talking up their growth potential from here, but their caution, writes Telis Demos.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Thousands of home buyers with adjustable mortgages are in for a nasty shock.

 

Tens of thousands of homeowners who used adjustable-rate mortgages to lock in historically low borrowing costs are now watching their monthly payments surge. Next year, 186,000 adjustable-rate mortgages will readjust. The largest category consists of people who took out seven-year adjustable rate mortgages in 2020, who will face a median payment hike of nearly $1,300 a month. Nicholas G. Miller reports on the buyers scrambling to pay down principal or trim household expenses to survive the spike.

 

5.

 

The brutal Harvard class everyone wants to take.

 

At Harvard, students are clamoring for a class that assigns a hefty book a week, requires regular essays and bans digital devices. The course is called Humanities 10 and it drew 180 applicants for just 90 spots this fall. Students, vying for the class, expressed the urge to be forced to tackle classics, sharpen their attention spans and think for themselves in the age of AI. One lecture on Jane Austen’s “Emma” even earned an applause. Pamela Paul sat in on the class to discover why old-school learning is suddenly so popular.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

How Anthropic arrived at its mind-boggling market opportunity.

 
 
 

Anthropic is giving new meaning to the concept of a total addressable market ahead of its initial public offering. Rather than explicitly listing a “total addressable market” figure, the AI company suggests it is staring down a $40 trillion opportunity. It arrived at the figure by targeting the global economic value of work performed by knowledge workers. Here’s a breakdown of how tech firms are turning everything from software spending to human labor into a measure of their potential market.

• The Fed announces its interest-rate decision. Our chief economics correspondent Nick Timiraos explains what he’s watching ahead of the Fed’s latest meeting.

 

• Apple holds a product-launch event in Los Angeles.

8. THE NUMBER

 
$6 billion
 

The estimated cost of building JPMorgan Chase’s new headquarters at 270 Park Avenue, according to the bank’s real-estate department. The bank has never officially disclosed the total price tag for the skyscraper, the tallest occupied office building in the U.S. Chief Executive Jamie Dimon has defended the spending as a worthwhile investment in shareholders’ best interests, despite once quipping that investors should short the stock of any company building a fancy new headquarters.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Merlot, after its celluloid humbling, is making a comeback.

 

Two decades ago, Paul Giamatti’s character infamously trashed the varietal in the hit movie “Sideways,” causing sales to tank and thousands of acres of California vines to be uprooted. Yet this mass culling actually did Merlot a favor by weeding out middling producers. Today, foodies and younger drinkers are embracing it.
